subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Eris: The Troublemaker
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Eris: The Troublemaker.

hook.text: Eris is slightly smaller than Pluto but 27% more massive. Its discovery forced Pluto's demotion.

buildup.text: Mike Brown found Eris in 2005 orbiting far beyond Pluto. He announced it as the tenth planet.

discovery.text: If Eris was a planet, so were Ceres, Makemake, and more. The planet count would keep climbing.

twist.text: Eris was named after the Greek goddess of discord—fitting for the object that threw astronomy into chaos.

climax.text: Brown wrote a book called 'How I Killed Pluto.' The discovery reshaped our definition of a planet.

punchline.text: One icy world forced astronomy to rewrite its rules.

quiz.question: Why did the discovery of Eris lead to Pluto's reclassification?
options: Eris was similar in size, forcing astronomers to define what counts as a planet
Eris collided with Pluto and shattered it into pieces
Eris was found to be a lost moon of Neptune

details.summary: Eris is a dwarf planet in the scattered disk beyond Neptune, slightly smaller than Pluto but 27% more massive. Its 2005 discovery by Mike Brown's team triggered the debate that led to Pluto's reclassification.
details.whyItMatters: Eris forced astronomers to define what a planet actually is. Without its discovery, Pluto would still be called the ninth planet. Eris reshaped planetary science by revealing the Kuiper Belt is richer and more complex than previously imagined.
takeaways: Eris is more massive than Pluto but slightly smaller in diameter
Its discovery triggered Pluto's reclassification as a dwarf planet
It orbits every 559 years at distances up to 97 AU from the Sun

faq.question: Why did Eris cause Pluto's reclassification?
faq.answer: Eris is more massive than Pluto, so if Pluto was a planet, Eris had to be one too. Rather than keep adding planets as more large Kuiper Belt objects were found, the IAU created the dwarf planet category in 2006 — demoting Pluto, classifying Eris, and establishing clear criteria for planethood.

faq.question: What do we know about Eris's surface?
faq.answer: Eris has an extremely bright, reflective surface — likely methane and nitrogen ice that freezes from its thin atmosphere when it's farthest from the Sun. It has one known moon, Dysnomia. At its current distance of about 96 AU, it's too far and faint for detailed study without future missions.
